title: Core boundary: how far "everything is a plugin" goes
ask: deepseek-harness says everything is a plugin. How much of that do we adopt: which parts are fixed core and which are plugins?
why: Decides how much of the system you can swap without touching core code. Hard to change once plugins exist.
learn: deepseek-harness (Cordis kernel about 2.7k lines plus loader about 1k; about 94 to 200 mounted rows; 328 packages); control-center plugins.toml; paperclip adapters. See Blueprint 8 and the research note on everything-is-a-plugin
rec_reason: Their kernel is small. Their weight is the packaging ceremony (one package per plugin, 209 empty companion files deleted, doc gates, a vendored kernel with 23 local changes). Copy the mechanism and leave the ceremony: a TypeScript kernel of about 500 lines, one repo of built-in plugins, config-only reload. Mark a few built-ins required, such as the file layer and the approval gate.

options.label: Plugin container kernel (the deepseek-harness idea, in TypeScript): about 500 lines of context tree, service registry with requires, scoped effects with dispose, and events. Everything else, including the verb registry, file layer, approval gate and workflow, is a built-in plugin that provides a service; a few are marked required
pros: One way to extend and to replace anything, including the file layer or the approval gate
The kernel stays tiny and stable; their Cordis core is about 2.7k lines in TypeScript
Each part is testable on its own
cons: More indirection to read and debug
A plugin waiting for a missing service stays pending silently unless startup lists it (their postmortems)
Required built-ins need protection so a swap cannot corrupt state
options.pick_if: you want to be able to replace any aspect, as you said.

options.label: Fixed core parts plus slots: loader, config merge, event bus, verb registry, file layer and approval gate are core; everything else plugs into named slots
pros: Core invariants (file layer, approval gate) stay fixed and safe
cons: Those core parts cannot be swapped without editing core
Two mechanisms: core parts and plugins
options.pick_if: safety matters more than total replaceability.

options.label: Fat core: tickets, UI and agents built in; plugins only for integrations
pros: Quickest path to a first version
cons: Replacing tickets or the workflow means editing core
The thing you said you want to avoid

options.label: The full deepseek-harness approach: a Cordis-style framework, one package per plugin, bundles, module hot reload, per-package README gates, bilingual docs
cons: 328 packages and heavy ceremony
Silent failures documented in their own postmortems
A vendored kernel to maintain
options.pick_if: you are building a platform for other people.

decided.note: Your message, 2026-10-07: go with the plugin container. A few built-ins (file layer, approval gate, verb registry) are marked required.

title: Extension points: which parts are swappable slots
ask: Which parts of the system get a named slot that a plugin can fill?
why: Each slot is a contract you must design, document and keep stable.
learn: control-center features/*.py; paperclip adapters; lc-wms config/*.toml vocabulary

options.label: Workflow: ticket stages, transitions, gates
Tickets: ticket model and storage
Artifact kinds and templates
options.desc: Decisions, bugs, gaps, specs and their templates.

options.label: CLI front-end
options.desc: Command names and shell UX over the same verbs.

options.label: Agent pack: roles and skills
Agent runtime adapter
Model provider adapter
Assistant (chat engine)
Voice (speech to text, text to speech)
Channels
Views: tabs, dashboard widgets, ticket page sections
Work log format
options.desc: TOML entries, markdown lines, or your own.

options.label: Scheduler
Importers and exporters
External tools through an MCP client
options.desc: Agents and the assistant call MCP servers.

decided.note: Your saved picks (plan-picks.json). worklog, sync, scheduler and mcp are slots with no v1 plugin (F18, F7e).

title: Plugin contract and packaging
ask: What is a plugin: a folder of configuration, a code module, or a separate process?
why: Decides who can make a plugin and how safe swapping is. Our declarative pack is deepseek-harness bundle: data only, mounts nothing itself.
learn: paperclip company packages (markdown + manifest); control-center feature modules; paperclip external adapters
rec_reason: Most swaps (statuses, roles, templates) are configuration, so they should need no code. Adapters (voice, channels) need code.

options.label: Two tiers: declarative packs (TOML + markdown + templates, no code) and code plugins (a TypeScript module exporting name, requires, a config schema and apply(ctx, config), F101)
options.desc: Both described by a plugin.toml manifest.
pros: Workflow, agent, template and theme swaps need no code
Packs are shareable as plain folders
Code only where it is really needed
cons: Two shapes to document and test

options.label: Code plugins only
cons: Changing statuses needs a developer
options.pick_if: plugins are always written by programmers.

options.label: Out-of-process plugins over JSON-RPC or MCP
options.desc: Each plugin is its own process.
cons: Process management and latency
Much more plumbing
options.pick_if: plugins come from people you do not trust.

decided.note: Your message, 2026-10-07: accept both. Packs are TOML, markdown and templates; code plugins are TypeScript modules.

title: Plugin settings and the settings screen
ask: How does a plugin declare its settings so the console can show a form?
why: Without this, every swap needs hand-built settings UI.

options.label: Manifest declares settings (type, default, label, secret flag); the Settings screen is generated; values live in workspace.toml; secrets by env-var name
options.desc: Declarative. A settings reference page is generated from the manifests, and each plugin states its known limitations (deepseek-harness practice).
pros: New plugins get a settings form for free
cons: A small schema to define and validate

options.label: Hand-built settings panel per plugin
cons: Work for every plugin
Inconsistent screens

options.label: Free-form [plugins.<id>] section in workspace.toml, edited by hand
cons: No validation, no form

title: Slot model: one active provider or many
ask: When a slot has several plugins, which one answers?
why: Decides whether swapping is a clear replacement or an ordering puzzle.
rec_reason: Declare cardinality per slot: one for workflow, tickets, assistant and voice; many for channels, views and adapters. Use the event bus for additive listeners. deepseek-harness evidence: one provider per service name, enforced loudly (a second registration fails the load); a singular name means one engine, a plural name means a registry; replacing means disable the old row and enable the new one.

options.label: Each slot declares its cardinality. One-active slots (workflow, tickets, assistant, voice) are swapped; many-active slots (channels, views, adapters) add up. Events cover extra listeners
cons: You must decide cardinality for every slot

options.label: Every slot allows many providers, all active
cons: Which assistant answers? Which workflow applies? Ordering rules grow

options.label: Only an event bus, no slots
cons: No guarantee a capability exists
Hard to swap and test

title: Workflow plugin: configurable ticket statuses
ask: Where do stages, transitions and gates live so you can change them without touching code?
why: This is your direct example: tickets changing status. The board, validator, agents and ticket page must all read the same definition.
learn: lc-wms config/board-ticket.toml, stages.toml; paperclip status transitions
rec_reason: Statuses are data. A declarative pack lets the board, agents and pages follow whatever workflow is active.

options.label: Declarative pack: workflow.toml lists stages, allowed transitions, gates and WIP limits. v1 ships lite (6 lanes); an lc-wms style pack (7 lanes) comes later; switch by swapping the pack
pros: Change statuses by editing one file
Board, agents, validator and ticket pages all follow it
cons: No stage name may be hard-coded anywhere
Switching packs needs a stage map for existing tickets
options.pick_if: you will adjust the lifecycle as you learn.

options.label: Stages hard-coded in core
cons: Fails your stated need
Every change is a code change

options.label: Workflow as code: a TypeScript state-machine plugin
cons: Hard to validate, share and draw
Needs a developer
options.pick_if: transitions need real logic (side effects, approvals).

title: Compatibility and versions
ask: How do you keep a plugin from breaking when the core changes?
why: A swappable system fails quietly if versions drift.
learn: deepseek-harness refuses files newer than the reader

options.label: Core API version; manifest declares requires_core and the slots it fills; incompatible plugins refuse to load with a clear message
pros: Clear failure instead of odd behaviour
cons: Core must keep a stable API number
options.pick_if: you plan to evolve the core.

options.label: No checks
cons: Silent breakage

options.label: Lockfile pinning exact plugin versions
cons: More ceremony

title: Trust and isolation
ask: How much do you trust plugins?
why: Plugins can run code and touch files; the approval gate must still apply.

options.label: Trusted in-process (your own plugins); risky actions still pass the core approval gate
cons: A bad plugin can do harm
options.pick_if: you write or review every plugin.

options.label: Out-of-process with a restricted workspace
cons: Heavy plumbing, esp. on Windows

options.label: Signed plugins
cons: Needs key handling

options.label: Capability declarations: a plugin lists what it needs (files, network, shell) and the core gate enforces it (paperclip style)
options.desc: Least privilege. Can be added on top of the trusted model.
pros: A plugin cannot quietly do more than it declared
Users see what a plugin wants before enabling it
cons: Capabilities must be designed and enforced in the core
options.pick_if: you will install plugins you did not write.

title: Sharing packs between workspaces
ask: How do you move a workflow, agent pack or template set from one workspace to another?
why: Paperclip exports a company as a markdown package with a fidelity report, secret scrubbing and collision handling. Our packs are folders already.

options.label: Packs are folders; share them through git (copy, subtree or submodule)
`hl pack export` and `hl pack install` with a report of what was not included, secrets scrubbed, collisions handled
A pack registry
Ship a few starter packs (delivery team, research team) installable at onboarding

title: Plugin form and kernel primitives
ask: What exactly is a plugin, and what does the kernel provide to it?
why: This is the contract every plugin author learns. Cordis shows a minimal set; a second plugin form caused a documented silent bug.
learn: deepseek-harness: module with name, inject, Config and apply(ctx, config); services, requires, effects, events; postmortem 0001 (a second form dropped inject)
rec_reason: One form only, validated at load. Four primitives are enough: a context tree with a service registry, requires that hold a plugin pending until its services exist (restarting dependents when a provider changes), effects that undo themselves on dispose, and events.

options.label: One plugin form: a module with name, requires (service keys), a config schema and apply(ctx, config); every registration returns a disposer so unloading undoes it; four kernel primitives: context tree with service registry, requires with dependent restart, scoped effects with dispose, events
options.desc: Mini Cordis in TypeScript: the same mechanism, small and typed.
pros: Dependency order comes from services, not hand-ordered lists
Clean unload and reload of any plugin
cons: The pending and restart logic is the subtle part and needs thorough tests
Authors must learn services and requires
options.pick_if: you accept a small kernel for total flexibility.

options.label: Plugins only register verbs and listen to events: no services, no requires
cons: A plugin cannot say it needs another capability
Swapping a provider is invisible to dependents
Order is by hand

options.label: Class-based plugins with init, start and stop methods and a manager
cons: Lifecycle bugs
Unwinding registrations by hand

title: How plugins talk: services, events and hook pipelines
ask: How does one plugin extend or intercept another?
why: Permissions, retries, logging and approvals are all interceptors. The mechanism decides how clean they are.
learn: deepseek-harness: 89 events (59 emit, 17 waterfall, 3 parallel, 2 serial); hooks like tools/pre-execute, tools/post-execute, agent/pre-step, approval/request; guard registry that can only deny
rec_reason: Capabilities are services. Behaviour hooks are named pipelines (domain/stage) with a declared mode. A separate guard registry can only deny, so no plugin order can undo a denial. Generate an event matrix so the vocabulary is documented.

options.label: Services for capabilities (ctx.tickets, ctx.llm). Hook pipelines named domain/stage with a declared mode: waterfall with next() for before and around, observe-only emit for results, parallel for flushes. A separate guard registry that can only deny. A generated event matrix
pros: Permissions, retries and logging become plugins
Denial cannot be undone by ordering
cons: Forgetting next() silently short-circuits (a bug class they call out)
The event vocabulary becomes semi-privileged and must stay documented

options.label: Plain events only: emit and listen, no ordering, no veto
cons: Plugins cannot modify or block an action
No ordering

options.label: A middleware chain per domain (koa style)
cons: deepseek-harness considered middleware and a phase state machine and chose events
One chain per domain is rigid
options.pick_if: there is one linear flow per domain.

title: Config as composition: rows, bundles and layers
ask: How is the set of plugins and their settings described, layered and changed?
why: This is where "replace any aspect" becomes a configuration edit. deepseek-harness composes everything from layered patches over a tree of rows.
learn: deepseek-harness profiles, bundles, cordis.patch.yml layers, --dump-config; its pain: silent no-op on an unmatched id, whole-config replacement pins values
rec_reason: Keep their model and fix their two pain points: an unmatched id is an error, and merge rules are explicit. Bundles are data-only presets (our declarative packs). `hl config show` explains every row and which layer supplied it.

options.label: The workspace mounts a tree of plugin rows (id, plugin, config, disabled) in workspace.toml; bundles are data-only presets of rows; ordered layers patch rows by id (bundle defaults, workspace.toml, workspace.local.toml, launch flags); an unmatched id is an error; explicit merge rules; `hl config show` prints the result with each row source layer
pros: A plugin swap is a one-row config edit
Fully explainable, and their silent failures are designed out
cons: More machinery than a flat list
Row ids must be kept stable
options.pick_if: you want swapping to be configuration.

options.label: A flat list of enabled plugin ids with settings (the earlier sketch)
cons: No layering, presets or per-row patching
Harder to explain where a value came from

options.label: deepseek-harness as is: YAML patch layers, a patch replaces a row whole config, unmatched ids ignored
cons: A typo in an id silently does nothing
Whole-config replacement pins values against later bundle updates
options.pick_if: never; copy the idea, not the sharp edges.

title: Ordering and priority
ask: When several plugins hook the same event, who runs first?
why: deepseek-harness had real bugs when order followed activation: tool order differed in CI, and equal prompt sections varied by platform.

options.label: An explicit integer priority on every hook and ordered list, with a deterministic tie-break (name); never rely on load order
Order follows activation order
Alphabetical by plugin name

title: Loud startup and diagnostics
ask: What happens when a plugin cannot start?
why: Their documented silent failures: a plugin pending forever with no error, a second export dropping requires, a config expression that never ran, patch ids that matched nothing.
rec_reason: Fail loudly and early. This is also the base for the doctor command (F63).

options.label: Startup lists every pending plugin with the service it waits for; a required-versus-optional audit; config validated at load with unknown keys refused; a second provider for one service name is a load error
Log and continue

title: Scoped contexts per agent and session
ask: Can one agent run with different tools and permissions from another?
why: deepseek-harness gives each agent and session its own child context and declarative presets, so a read-only reviewer and a builder differ cleanly.

options.label: Child contexts per agent or run (ctx.child(scope)) with their own tool list and guards; agent presets are small declarative trees
One global set for every agent

title: Reload and dormant plugins
ask: Do changes apply without a restart, and can a plugin sit idle until configured?
why: deepseek-harness reloads config live, keeps some plugins dormant until settings supply routes, and is proposing to drop code hot reload (about 400 lines plus 372 of tests).

options.label: Config reload only (no code reload); plugins can be mounted dormant until configured; provider settings re-read per request; restart for code changes
options.desc: Most of the value, little code.

options.label: Full hot reload of plugin code
Restart on any change

title: Plugin conventions and generated docs
ask: Which of deepseek-harness plugin habits do we keep, in lite form?
learn: deepseek-harness: package README gates, generated config catalog and event matrix, real-loader composition tests, dispose tests

options.label: A short README per plugin: purpose, config, extension points, Known limitations
A generated config reference and event matrix from manifests and declarations
Each plugin has a test that mounts it through the real loader, and a dispose test
Decisions recorded as short notes: problem, decision, alternatives, consequences (their Agent Notes)
Heavy gates: bilingual docs, 100% coverage, 68 verify scripts

title: Plugin languages: TypeScript, and other languages?
ask: The stack is TypeScript everywhere. May a plugin be written in another language, for example Python for local speech or vision?
why: Some adapters (local speech, vision) have their best libraries outside JavaScript. A clear rule keeps the core simple and the door open.
learn: control-center desktop sidecar (Python with whisper and piper); deepseek-harness plugins; F42
rec_reason: Plugins are TypeScript modules in the same workspace. Another language runs as a separate process that talks to the core through the CLI or a small JSON contract, so the kernel never embeds a second runtime.

options.label: Plugins are TypeScript modules; any other language runs as a separate process that uses the CLI or a small JSON contract (for example local speech in Python)
pros: The kernel stays small and single-language
Python speech and vision libraries stay usable
The control-center sidecar idea carries over
cons: Two runtimes on a machine that uses such a plugin

options.label: TypeScript plugins only
cons: No local speech or vision libraries

options.label: Embed a Python runtime inside the kernel
cons: Heavy, fragile on Windows, two dependency worlds
